passage:
My name is Kiran, and one Sunday I lay on the sofa with a comic. Kashish Masi walked in and said, "Lying around again? Lazy." Then she looked at Papa, who had come home at ten the night before and was also stretched on the sofa, and said, "Poor thing, he works so hard."
My cheeks burned. I put the comic down and hunted for something useful to do, even though my head was tired from a week of tests.
Later, at a friend's house, everybody flopped on the floor with cushions and nobody apologised. I noticed that.

qa.q: What did Kashish Masi say to Kiran on the sofa?
qa.a: She said, 'Lying around again? Lazy.'

qa.q: What did Kiran feel when Masi called Kiran lazy but praised Papa?
qa.a: Hurt and ashamed. Kiran's cheeks burned and Kiran hurried to find something useful despite being tired.

qa.q: What could Kashish Masi have said instead?
qa.a: She could have asked how the week of tests went and let Kiran rest, treating rest the same way she treats Papa's.

qa.q: How might Papa see the difference between his rest and Kiran's?
qa.a: He may not notice it. He is resting after a late night and is praised, so the unfairness is invisible to him.

grounding: A child hears that resting is lazy while a busy adult is praised.

passage:
Note from Baljeet, class 5 teacher. At break today Naveen lay on the grass under the neem tree with his eyes closed. When I came near he jumped up and said, "Sorry, ma'am, I'm not being lazy." I asked who called it lazy. He said his aunt at home says resting is for lazy people, and that his father is proud to work every Sunday.
I sat beside him and said resting is how the body and mind get ready for work. He looked doubtful but lay back down. I will speak gently to his parents at the next meeting, and give the class a quiet minute after PT.

qa.q: Where did Naveen lie down at break?
qa.a: On the grass under the neem tree.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel when Baljeet came near?
qa.a: Guilty and worried. He jumped up and apologised, saying he was not being lazy.

qa.q: What did Baljeet do that could help Naveen?
qa.a: Baljeet sat beside him, said resting readies the body and mind for work, and planned to speak gently to his parents and give the class a quiet minute.

qa.q: How might Naveen's aunt see resting, judging from what Naveen says?
qa.a: She seems to link rest with laziness and work with worth, so she may not realise her words make Naveen feel guilty.

grounding: A child hears that resting is lazy and a teacher shows that rest is respected.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 5, Friday.
Sumit asked to see me because he "can't stop". During break he walks round and round the corridor instead of sitting with friends. He said, "If I sit, it means I'm lazy. My uncle says only lazy people lie down in the afternoon. Papa works fourteen hours and everyone says he's great."
He looked ashamed saying he feels tired after school.
I told him rest is part of working well, like the break in a cricket match. I've asked his parents to come in on Monday to talk about afternoon downtime.
Uday

qa.q: What does Sumit do during break instead of sitting?
qa.a: He walks round and round the corridor.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel about being tired after school?
qa.a: He felt ashamed, believing that resting means he is lazy.

qa.q: What did Uday do next?
qa.a: Uday told Sumit rest is part of working well, like a break in cricket, and asked his parents to come in on Monday.

qa.q: What would change if Sumit's family respected afternoon rest?
qa.a: Sumit could sit with friends and rest after school without feeling ashamed.

grounding: Shows a child who hears rest called lazy while a busy adult is praised, and feels unable to stop without shame.

passage:
Saturday
Ammi called me lazy again today because I was lying on the sofa reading after my exams. Then she told Auntie on the phone how Nitin Bhaiya studies till midnight and "never wastes a minute". I put the book down and pretended to tidy my shelf so nobody would say anything.
But I was so tired. I did six exams this week!
In the evening Abbu came home, saw me tidying the same shelf, and said, "Farida, exams are over. Go and read your book, you've earned it." He even lay down on the other sofa and closed his eyes. Ammi laughed at both of us, but she didn't say lazy again.
Farida

qa.q: How many exams did Farida do this week?
qa.a: Six exams.

qa.q: Why did Farida pretend to tidy the shelf?
qa.a: Farida felt ashamed of resting after being called lazy, and wanted to avoid more criticism.

qa.q: What did Abbu do that helped?
qa.a: Abbu said the rest was earned and lay down on the other sofa himself, showing that rest is normal.

qa.q: How might Ammi see rest after Abbu's example?
qa.a: Ammi laughed and stopped calling it lazy, perhaps seeing that rest after hard work is fair.

grounding: Shows a child told that resting is lazy while a busy sibling is praised, and a parent making downtime respectable.

passage:
In the small town of Tenali, summer afternoons were for sleeping. Yamini, ten, lay on the cool floor with a comic after helping her mother, Keerthana, at the tailoring shop all morning. A neighbour peered in through the window. "So lazy, this girl! My Swathi is at tuition even now."
Yamini sat up fast, face hot.
Keerthana didn't look up from her sewing machine. "She worked since seven. In our house, afternoon is rest." She said it simply, like the weather.
The neighbour left. Yamini lay back down slowly. Her mother hummed. After a while Yamini turned the page, and the heat in her face went away.

qa.q: Where did Yamini help in the morning?
qa.a: At the tailoring shop, with her mother, Keerthana.

qa.q: Why did Yamini's face go hot?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and ashamed when the neighbour called her lazy.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana's calm answer help Yamini?
qa.a: It stated the family's rule, that afternoon is rest after work, without arguing, so Yamini could rest without shame.

qa.q: How does the neighbour see Yamini's rest?
qa.a: The neighbour sees it as laziness, comparing her with a child still at tuition.

grounding: Shows a child called lazy for resting, and a household that respects downtime letting her stop without shame.

passage:
In their Nairobi house, Wanjiru, nine, lay on the sofa after school with a comic. Her father came in and sighed. "Lying around again? Look at your uncle Otieno. Up at five, two jobs, never sits down. That's how you get ahead."
Wanjiru sat up quickly and pretended to look for her homework. Her cheeks burned. Resting felt like something she had to hide.
That weekend her aunt Nour visited. After lunch, Nour stretched out on the veranda mat. "Come, Wanjiru. Rest with me. We've both worked hard this week."
Wanjiru hesitated. "Isn't that lazy?"
"Resting isn't lazy. It's how you have energy for the good things," Nour said, closing her eyes. "Even Otieno sleeps."
Wanjiru lay down beside her. The sun was warm. For the first time in weeks, she didn't feel guilty for stopping.

qa.q: How many jobs does uncle Otieno have?
qa.a: Uncle Otieno has two jobs.

qa.q: Why did Wanjiru's cheeks burn when her father spoke?
qa.a: Wanjiru felt ashamed, as though resting were something bad she had to hide.

qa.q: What could a parent say instead to respect a child's downtime?
qa.a: Something like Nour's words: resting after school isn't lazy, it's how you get energy for the good things.

qa.q: How does Nour see rest?
qa.a: Nour sees rest as normal and earned, relaxing openly and inviting Wanjiru to rest without guilt.

grounding: A child told resting is lazy while a busy adult is praised feels ashamed, and an aunt who respects downtime helps her stop without shame.
